rules.plain_language_rule: Periodisation organizes training into planned blocks to produce specific physical adaptations.
Training variables should be manipulated according to the desired adaptation rather than changed randomly.
A microcycle is generally a weekly training block containing the individual sessions performed during that week.
A mesocycle contains multiple microcycles and generally targets a broader training objective over approximately 2–8 weeks.
Every microcycle should serve the objective of the larger mesocycle.
Microcycles must remain flexible enough to respond to readiness, match demands, injury status, and unexpected changes.
The system must preserve both planned training and actual completed training.
Daily modifications should preserve the larger training objective whenever practical.
Physical qualities may be developed, maintained, restored, or de-emphasized depending on the current block.
Training sessions should be nested within microcycles, microcycles within mesocycles, and mesocycles within the larger season plan.
Every exercise or drill should be traceable to a session objective, microcycle objective, mesocycle objective, and athlete need.
Rugby periodisation must account for frequent competition and cannot rely on perfectly rigid linear planning.
Match schedule, recovery, travel, and training constraints should influence weekly planning.
Planned workload and actual workload should be recorded separately so future programming can respond to what the athlete actually experienced.

master_rule_source_variants.plain_language_rule: Screening should progress from broad observation toward more specific testing.
ROM tests provide local joint-level information.
Dynamic tests show how the athlete controls movement under more demanding conditions.
A movement finding generates hypotheses; it does not prove a muscular cause.
Repeated findings across different assessments strengthen a working hypothesis.
Secondary isolation tests should be used to confirm or challenge suspected contributors.
Corrective interventions should match the actual limitation: mobility, strength, stability/control, or technique.
Pain changes the pathway from coaching/correction to medical review.
Every assessment must be standardized enough to allow reliable longitudinal comparison.
The original test should be repeated after intervention to verify whether the athlete actually improved.

master_rule_policy: Preserve supplied wording for reconciliation; do not count as additional unique master identifiers.
